title: Too much advice
hook: Three people, three different answers. Here's how to stay calm and know who to ask.

screens.text: By now someone has probably corrected how you pray. Then someone else said the opposite. It's confusing, and it can make you feel like you're doing everything wrong. You're not. Today: how to handle it.
**Why answers differ.** Most people who correct you mean well. And on many small details of prayer, scholars have honestly differed for over a thousand years. Different isn't wrong.
bubbles: There are four main schools of law (each is a **madhab**). They differ on small things, like where to hold your hands, and all four are valid.

screens.situation: After Dhuhr at the masjid, three kind people come over. Dre says you should raise your hands again before bowing. An older man says no, only at the start. Tyler says don't trust anyone: look up the hadith yourself. What do you do?

options.text: Go with whoever sounded most sure
options.feedback: Understandable, but sounding sure isn't the same as knowing. Ask someone trained, then relax.

options.text: Search hadith online tonight and decide for yourself
options.feedback: Scholars train for years to do that well. Two weeks in, it usually leads to more confusion, not less.

options.text: Say "Thank you, I'll check with my imam," ask {{mentor.name}} or the imam, and keep your masjid's way meanwhile
options.feedback: Yes. Both hand practices are valid in different schools. One trusted teacher and your masjid's practice keep you steady.

options.text: Stop going to the masjid so nobody corrects you
options.feedback: That would cost you a lot. Corrections can be handled kindly. Your masjid is still where your people are.

screens.text: **Pick one trusted source.** The Qur'an tells people who don't know to ask those who do [Q 16:43]. So: one teacher, {{mentor.name}} or your imam, and your masjid's way while you learn.
bubbles: Once, people gave an injured man a ruling without knowledge, and it harmed him. The Prophet ﷺ said they should have asked, because asking is the cure for not knowing [Abu Dawud 336].

screens.prompt: Which are good places to take a question about how to pray?

options.feedback: Right. A real, trained person who knows you and your masjid.

options.text: This app's AI guide, which can pass hard questions to your imam
options.feedback: Right. It answers the basics and sends personal or disputed questions to your imam.

options.text: The angriest video in your feed
options.feedback: Not quite. Harsh online voices often argue over small things. They're a common source of convert burnout.

options.text: Whoever corrects you most often at the masjid
options.feedback: Not quite. Thank them kindly, but check with your teacher. Frequent advice isn't the same as qualified advice.

screens.text: **Today, al-Fatiha is whole.** You learned it verse by verse this week. From now on, recite all of **al-Fatiha** in every rak'ah, instead of the remembrance phrases (dhikr) you used while learning.
bubbles: If a verse slips during prayer, say what you remember and carry on.
In the first two rak'ahs, a short **surah** (chapter) follows it. Your first one, **al-Ikhlas**, comes on Days 17–18.

screens.prompt: Put al-Fatiha in order, starting with the Bismillah you say before it.
screens.feedback: That's the whole chapter, in the order you'll recite it in every rak'ah.

variant.default: **Amin.** After al-Fatiha, say ***Amin*** ("O Allah, answer our prayer"). The Prophet ﷺ told people praying behind an imam to say Amin with him [Bukhari 780]. {{masjid.name}} will show you whether to say it aloud or quietly.
variant.hanafi: **Amin.** After al-Fatiha, say ***Amin*** ("O Allah, answer our prayer") **quietly**, under your breath. Behind an imam, you don't recite al-Fatiha yourself: you listen, and when he finishes it, you say Amin quietly [Bukhari 780; First Instructions on Worship ch. 7].

screens.title: Recitation self-check (2 minutes, not during prayer)

steps.text: Play the al-Fatiha audio at the end of today's lesson once, and just listen
Say it aloud slowly, one verse at a time, along with the audio
Now say it without the audio. Which verse made you pause? Repeat that one three times
Check the long sounds: the long vowels in al-'alamin, ar-rahman, ar-rahim, maliki and ad-dallin are stretched, not clipped
Say it once more, start to finish, then Amin
Optional: record yourself, or ask {{mentor.name}} to listen once this week

screens.done_text: That's real progress. Small slips are normal; the one who struggles with the Qur'an still gets rewarded.

prayerPhrase.translit: Bismillahir-rahmanir-rahim. Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin. Ar-rahmanir-rahim. Maliki yawmid-din. Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in. Ihdinas-siratal-mustaqim. Siratal-ladhina an'amta 'alayhim, ghayril-maghdubi 'alayhim wa lad-dallin. Amin
prayerPhrase.meaning: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All praise is for Allah, Lord of all the worlds, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, Master of the Day of Judgment. It is You we worship and You we ask for help. Guide us to the straight path: the path of those You have favored, not of those who earned Your anger, nor of those gone astray. Amin (O Allah, answer our prayer)
prayerPhrase.when: While standing, in every rak'ah, then Amin, the way your masjid says it. [Q 1:1–7; Amin: Bukhari 780]

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Differences in prayer details between the four schools are normal and valid; all four accept praying behind an imam of another school [Research Notes - Core Essentials and Madhab Map, common-ground section; AMJA 78081].
- Common ground across scholars: a convert shouldn't derive rulings personally from hadith; learn from a qualified, accessible teacher; follow the masjid's practice while learning; don't let small differences cause conflict [SeekersGuidance (choosing a school); IslamQA 21420; Welcome to Islam D5]. `Q10` is open: whether formally following one madhab is required.
- Ask those who know [Q 16:43]; asking is the cure for not knowing [Abu Dawud 336, hasan per al-Albani].
- Honest mistakes made while learning, including following another school's way by accident, aren't sins [SeekersGuidance (convert following a school)].
- From today the convert recites the whole of al-Fatiha in every rak'ah (Q2's drafted timeline). Hanafi: al-Fatiha is wajib and some recitation is fard; a short surah after it in the first two rak'ahs of obligatory prayers is wajib (al-Ikhlas arrives Days 17–18; a new Muslim is excused for what they haven't learned yet, Qibla 35467). Rak'ahs 3–4: al-Fatiha only [First Instructions on Worship ch. 7].
- Amin: Hanafi says it quietly; a Hanafi follower doesn't recite al-Fatiha behind the imam and says Amin quietly when the imam finishes it [First Instructions on Worship ch. 7; Bukhari 780].

**Likely questions**
- *"Someone said my prayer is invalid because I [hold my hands / raise my hands / sit] differently."* If it matches the masjid's taught practice, it's a valid school's practice. Reassure; suggest checking specifics with the imam. Never declare anyone's prayer invalid.
- *"Which madhab should I follow?"* Give the common ground (follow the masjid's practice while learning from a qualified local teacher); say scholars differ on whether choosing one formally is required; offer "Ask my imam" (Q10).
- *"Why do people at other masjids say Amin out loud?"* Shafi'is and Hanbalis say it aloud in the prayers recited aloud; Hanafis say it quietly; both are valid.
- *"I keep mixing up verses."* Offer a slow verse-by-verse drill outside prayer; remind them the struggling reciter is rewarded [Muslim 798].
- *"Can I just read Fatiha off my phone in prayer?"* No (Q2): practice before and after, never during.

**Escalate:** a specific dispute the convert is stuck in; anyone pressuring them to join a group or reject their masjid; harsh or repeated public correction (route to the mentor, kindly).

**Don't**
- Don't take sides between schools or call any of the four wrong.
- Don't encourage the convert to research rulings from hadith on their own.
- Don't disparage the people who corrected them; most mean well.
madhabNote:
- **Amin:** Shafi'is and Hanbalis say it aloud in the prayers recited aloud (Fajr, Maghrib, Isha), the imam and followers together; Hanafis and Malikis say it quietly (in the Maliki school, the imam of a prayer recited aloud doesn't say it at all).
- **Al-Fatiha behind the imam:** Hanafis don't recite it at all; Malikis recite it only in the silent prayers; Shafi'is recite it in every rak'ah; Hanbalis recommend it in the silent prayers. Day 22 covers praying behind an imam.
- **Raising the hands** (the scenario): Hanafis and Malikis raise them only at the opening takbir; Shafi'is and Hanbalis also raise them before and after bowing. All are valid.
